Methodology

From market data to daily aggregate profitability

The tracker estimates revenues and costs for GB gas-fired generation and calculates the difference as aggregate generation profit.

Aggregate profit
A sector-level estimate of generation profitability rather than accounting profits of individual companies.

Estimates are based on the methodology developed by Egorov et al. (2026).

The tracker uses the methodology developed in Egorov et al. (2026) to estimate annual profits of the GB gas power generators over the period 2019–2024.

The research behind the tracker.

Evaluation of aggregate profits of GB gas power stations by Aleksei Egorov, Chrysanthi Rapti, Margaux Daly, and Michael Grubb, UCL Institute for Sustainable Resources.
The research

What happened to gas-generator profits during the energy crisis?

The study examines whether the exceptional increase in electricity prices in 2021–2022 was fully explained by higher input costs.
Main findings

An exceptional, but temporary, profitability shock

1

Profits rose much faster than costs

Aggregate profits increased from roughly £0.5–0.6 billion in 2019–2020 to £2.9 billion in 2021 and £4.7 billion in 2022.

2

Crisis-period margins exceeded normal benchmarks

Estimated profit margins reached 19% in 2021 and 18% in 2022, compared with a benchmark range of approximately 7–10%.

3

The explanation is more complex than fuel costs

Higher gas and carbon prices were the initial driver of higher electricity prices, but they do not fully explain the scale of the increase in generator profitability.

4

Interconnectors mattered particularly in 2022

Exceptional conditions in continental Europe, particularly France, contributed to GB electricity prices becoming disconnected from comparatively cheaper domestic gas.
